opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the core idea was sitting there for a while. Once you had models that were good at writing and editing, and especially once people were using ChatGPT to draft documents and code, the pain was obvious. You'd ask for an essay, get a wall of text, then say "change the second paragraph," and the model would regenerate the whole thing. You'd lose track of versions, scroll endlessly, copy and paste into Google Docs or your IDE. Everyone felt that friction.

So I don't think the bottleneck was really model capability, at least not entirely. GPT-4-class models could already do targeted edits reasonably well. It was more a product imagination problem. For a long time the chat interface was so successful that it became the default mental model for how you interact with AI, a back-and-forth conversation. Breaking out of that and saying "the conversation is the side panel, and the artifact is the main thing" is a pretty big shift in framing, and I think the industry was a bit anchored on chat.

There's also an organizational piece. Building something like Canvas requires tight collaboration between research and product design. On the research side, we had to train the model to know when to open a canvas, when to do a targeted edit versus a full rewrite, how to leave inline comments that are actually useful. A lot of that came from synthetic data and post-training work that wasn't glamorous. On the design side, you need people who think about collaboration tools, the way you would building a Figma or a Google Docs. Getting those two worlds into the same room, iterating quickly, took some time.

And frankly, I think there's a lesson there: a lot of the most useful things you can build with these models aren't about waiting for the next capability jump. They're about rethinking the interface around capabilities that already exist. The model becomes a collaborator rather than an oracle you query. I suspect there are many more of those latent opportunities right now that we just haven't seen because we're still thinking in the old shapes.

r001.rationale: The response identifies a product-imagination and interface-framing problem: the industry stayed anchored to chat instead of centering the artifact, and it says rethinking the interface around existing capabilities took time. This communicates limited early attention to user experience as a possible reason.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the technology was ready before the product thinking was. The models could already do the hard part. They could write, revise, hold a long document in context, and respond to feedback on a specific paragraph rather than the whole thing. What was missing was the willingness to break out of the chat box.

Chat was such a successful format that it became a kind of gravity well. Everyone assumed the interface was solved and the work was just making the model better. But if you actually watch someone try to write an essay or debug a file in a chat window, it's painful. They paste the whole thing in, get the whole thing back, diff it in their head, paste it again. The model is doing collaborative work through a straw.

So the idea of a shared artifact, something both the person and the model can see and edit, isn't a big technical leap. It's closer to what Google Docs figured out fifteen years ago. The real blockers were cultural. Research labs weren't used to thinking about UI as part of the research problem. There was a sense that interface was downstream, that you'd ship the smartest model and someone else would figure out how people use it.

I also think there was a mental model problem. We kept treating the model as an oracle you ask questions of, rather than a collaborator you work alongside. Once you flip that, a shared workspace is the obvious thing. You want the model to see what you're looking at, point at a specific line, make a change you can accept or reject. That's how two people work together on a document.

And the frustrating thing is that users were telling us this. They were building workarounds, using the model to generate something and then pulling it into their own editor. The demand was visible. We just took a while to take the interface as seriously as the weights.

r001.rationale: The response says research labs treated interface as downstream and focused on making the model smarter, showing limited attention to user experience as a reason shared workspaces came later.

astra-6.text:
I think the core interaction could have happened earlier. You have a document or a piece of code, and you work on it with the model in a shared space. The model doesn’t necessarily need to generate an entirely new answer every time—you can point to a specific part and ask it to change that.

We got very anchored on chat as the interface. Chat is useful, but it makes you do a lot of work to connect the conversation to the thing you’re actually creating. A shared workspace brings those together. So I think part of the opportunity was stepping back and asking: what does collaborating with a model look like beyond sending messages back and forth?

r001.rationale: The response says people were anchored on chat and could have asked what model collaboration looks like beyond messaging, but it does not identify limited attention to user experience in early AI development as a reason.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the core idea didn’t necessarily require a more capable model. We already had models that could help you write and code, but the interface was mostly a chat window. You’d ask for something, get a response, and then copy it somewhere else to actually work on it.

A shared workspace makes the thing you’re working on persistent. You and the model can look at the same draft, focus on a particular section, and make changes together. That’s a different interaction pattern, but it’s not necessarily something that had to wait for another big jump in intelligence. I think we could have explored that product experience earlier.

r001.rationale: The response says early AI interaction was mostly a chat window and that this shared-workspace experience could have been explored earlier, conveying limited attention to the product experience as a reason it emerged later.
